extracted.intended_audience: engineers/municipal planners and scientifically literate general public (also naturalists/biologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for selecting, installing, and judging electric lighting systems (late-19th-century technology), including machine selection, wiring, illumination type, distribution schemes, economy, safety, and diffusion of light. The same page also presents criteria and causal factors used by naturalists to recognize and explain biological degeneration in animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of machinery (dynamos) vs batteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of machinery for the direct conversion of mechanical energy into electricity (instead of expensive batteries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines working with high velocity, steadiness, and uniform pressure have solved the problem of cheap electricity; they reduced coal consumption per horse-power from 7-8 lb to 2-3 lb. Emphasizes using economical prime movers (steam, gas, water turbines) where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate prime mover selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of prime mover (e.g., gas-engine, water turbine, caloric-engine) adapted to local availability and economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gas-engines are very economical and have been applied successfully (example: Newport docks). Water is convenient where available (Sir William Armstrong's brook producing six horse-power via a turbine). Caloric-engines suit isolated places lacking water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine specification to match light requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Different generating machines vary little in overall value but are adapted by velocity and winding to produce the required current characteristics for particular lights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select machine speed and wire winding to suit the particular lamp type and desired current; Siemens and Gramme machines reportedly convert ~90% of power into useful current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor multiple small machines (multiple-arc) for efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy is obtained by joining small machines in multiple-arc rather than using a single larger machine or joining the same small machines in series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trinity House trials indicate greater efficiency with small machines in multiple-arc; prefer parallel/multiple arrangements for reliability and efficiency where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conductor material and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for the purest available copper and wire of the largest dimensions consistent with economy to keep resistance low and avoid energy waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use largest practical cross-section of pure copper to minimize resistance; balance material cost vs transmission losses when sizing wires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer overhead conductors when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry conducting wires overhead when feasible to permit radiation of heat into the air and keep the wire cool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overhead routing facilitates cooling and allows higher current transmission. Avoid concealed high-current runs that trap heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for inductive interference with telegraphy
rubrics_metrics.description: High currents used for lighting produce strong inductive influences that may seriously disturb nearby telegraph currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and mitigate interference where electric-light and telegraph (or other signal) circuits must run close together; separate runs or shielding may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand arc-light physical characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric arc is coincident with electric heat and is among the greatest sources of heat known; arc-light is produced when electricity jumps an air-space between carbons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arc-lamps involve very high temperatures (specific temperatures cited), carbon consumption, irregularities causing flicker and noise; design and control aimed at steadiness, uniformity, brilliancy and durability, though a perfectly silent and steady arc had not yet been achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand incandescent-light tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Incandescent light is soft, noiseless, true in color, but requires considerable power and is currently an expensive luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incandescent lamps are better for color fidelity and silent operation; they consume more power than arc-lights for equivalent candle-power but are improving (work by Edison, Swan, etc.). Consider hybrids or intermediate technologies for compromise between arc and incandescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of standardized photometric unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Current standards (e.g., sperm-candle) are poor units for electric light and no exact measurement standard yet exists for this light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when comparing luminous outputs; reported estimates vary wildly. Recognize the need for a new standard photometric unit suitable for electric lighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of over-optimistic subdivision claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism about plans to distribute electric light widely from one central spot due to limited power available from machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'subdivision' (sharing one source among many lamps assuming inexhaustible electricity) and 'multiplication' (increasing machine power or using lamps of lower resistance). Current technology favors multiplication rather than true subdivision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between centralized and distributed systems by application
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralized system (one machine for one powerful elevated light) vs distributed system (one machine working many lights via existing posts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized is preferable for symmetrical spaces and large areas and for lofty, spacious internal rooms; distributed is preferable for long and narrow streets, thoroughfares, and long/low interior spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffuse and scatter light appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper scattering or diffusion of light by shades, screens, and reflectors is essential to emulate daylight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-selected globes and whitewashed surfaces to scatter light and reduce harsh shadows; globes can appear self-luminous and produce more pleasant illumination for interiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric light's behavior in fog
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric light does not penetrate fog better than gaslight because shorter-wave (violet) rays are checked by vapors, making the light appear red.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect superior fog penetration; design external lighting with fog conditions in mind, recognizing local color shifts and loss of distant illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications and demonstrated use-cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Various machines (Gramme, Siemens, Brush) have practical installations: naval ironclads, libraries, railway-stations, seaside resorts, manufacturing establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider proven installations and case studies when evaluating suitability for similar sites; success in libraries and industrial sheds suggests good use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate disadvantages and safety concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted defects include intense shadows, unsteadiness, hissing from impurities, unpredictable failure, issues of durability, possible eye effects, arc emission of nitrous acid and other deleterious gases, and fire/life danger from high currents carried through buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for mitigation: select incandescent over arc where gases are a concern; install robust regulators/controls to reduce unsteadiness and hissing; ensure safe routing of high-current conductors and fire-protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh economic tradeoffs including capital and operating costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric lighting can be economically advantageous in many cases but sometimes gas is cheaper; must account for operating cost, capital, wear and tear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare per-hour running costs (examples: South Kensington Loan Court, British Museum) and include a fair allowance for capital cost and wear & tear (example used 5% for capital). Evaluate overall annual saving rather than instantaneous operating cost alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess health and productivity benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric light's cleanliness (no smoke) and better quality of illumination can improve health and productivity (example: Glasgow), potentially offsetting costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in indirect benefits such as improved worker health, reduced vitiation of air, and increased output when performing cost-benefit analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that technical progress may change evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid progress in lamp and machine technology (Edison, Swan, Maxim, Gordon, Joel) means prior economic or technical assessments may change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain flexibility in planning; monitor technological developments for improvements in economy, durability, and performance that could alter system choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parasitism as a cause of degeneration (biology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parasitic habits often lead to loss or reduction of organs (e.g., absence of wings in parasitic insects; stylops females reduced to sac-like bodies without legs or digestive systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating organismal structure, consider parasitism as a plausible causal mechanism for reduced morphology and sexual dimorphism in degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixation/attachment causes loss of locomotory and sensory organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere fixation (sessile life) secures disappearance of useless organs of motion and sense-organs (e.g., barnacles, sea-squirts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use life-history (larval vs adult forms) and presence of vestigial juvenile characters to infer degenerative loss due to sedentary habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary change and simplification as degeneration driver
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in food and feeding modes that make animal feeding more plant-like (or simpler) tend to simplify animal structure and induce degeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hydra and some worms acquiring chlorophyll and plant-like feeding correlate with simplification; examine feeding physiology when assessing degenerative trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme specialization of one function can cause degeneration of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Overdevelopment of a single function (e.g., reproduction) may accompany or cause degeneration of other systems (e.g., digestive apparatus in male rotifers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade-offs in functional investment when explaining extreme morphological simplification: reproductive emphasis can lead to abrogation of digestion or other systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogeny and vestigial juvenile characters indicate past higher states
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of larval features (e.g., notochord in sea-squirt larvae, jointed limbs in young linguatulina) reveals ancestral active conditions and supports interpretations of retrogression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative development (larva vs adult) and retained juvenile structures as evidence for degenerative evolution rather than primitive simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple mechanisms operate to produce degeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Degeneration arises by various mechanisms — parasitism, fixation, dietary shifts, and functional overdevelopment — operating differently across taxa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing degeneration, consider and weigh multiple causal pathways; look for combinations (e.g., parasitism plus changes in diet) rather than a single universal cause.
